=== Project 58000- Update Transmission Cost Recovery TAEBA Comments August 11.pdf ===
                                            PROJECT NO. 58000

     RULE MAKING TO UPDATE WHOLESALE                   §
                                                                     PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
     AND IOU RETAIL TRANSMISSION COST                  §
                                                                             OF TEXAS
       RECOVERY IN THE ERCOT REGION                    §

  COMMENTS OF TEXAS ADVANCED ENERGY BUSINESS ALLIANCE IN RESPONSE TO COMMISSION
                               STAFF’S PROPOSAL


Texas Advanced Energy Business Alliance (“TAEBA”) hereby submits these comments on Commission Staff’s
Memo and Proposal for Publication filed on July 10, 2026, in the above-referenced project. TAEBA
includes local and national advanced energy companies seeking to make Texas’ energy system secure,
clean, reliable, and affordable. Advanced energy technologies include energy efficiency, energy storage,
demand response, solar, wind, hydro, nuclear, and electric vehicles. Used together, these technologies and
services will create and maintain a higher-performing energy system - one that is reliable, resilient,
diverse, and cost-effective - while also improving the availability and quality of customer-facing services.
TAEBA’s membership also includes advanced energy buyers, representing the interests of large electricity
consumers interested in increasing their purchases of advanced energy to meet specific energy offtake
needs.

TAEBA evaluates transmission cost recovery policies based on three core principles: (1) policies should
incentivize reductions in peak demand, which lowers total system costs for all customers; (2) price signals
should be preserved to encourage efficient behavior and investment; and (3) policies should not
discourage flexible load participation, which is increasingly critical to maintaining grid reliability in ERCOT.

General Comments

TAEBA supports the Commission’s decision to maintain the coincident peak (“CP”) methodology. As TAEBA
has stated in previous comments, the CP methodology provides an important price signal that incentivizes
demand response during the highest system peaks. Reducing demand during these peak periods lowers
overall system costs by reducing the need for new transmission investment, benefiting all customers. While
TAEBA continues to believe that a 5CP approach would be the best of the previously considered options,
12CP remains acceptable.

TAEBA continues to have serious concerns with requiring large loads to pay a minimum billing demand
based on 100% of a large load customer’s contracted peak demand. In Project No. 58484, the

Texas Advanced Energy Business Alliance                                             P.O. Box 301151, Austin, TX 78703
                                                                                             TexasAdvancedEnergy.org
 recommendation under discussion was for a 10- to 15-year period, with the applicable percentage of
contracted peak demand still to be determined. In this proposal, the length of the minimum billing demand
has been increased to 20 years, with the minimum billing demand set at 100% of contracted peak
demand.

A 100% contracted peak demand charge appears to be an outlier compared to emerging large load
tariff proposals in other jurisdictions. According to a database of emerging large load tariffs, of the 77
filings catalogued, only 33 included any minimum billing demand requirement.1 Of those 33 filings, the
average minimum billing demand was 80% of contracted peak load, with only one utility setting a 100%
minimum billing demand.2 Between the 100% minimum billing demand, the 20-year duration, and billing
commencing whether or not the large load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity, the
proposal could impose significant costs and risks on large load customers and discourage investment in
Texas.

The 100% minimum billing demand could also create reliability and affordability concerns for ERCOT and
Texas customers. Without the ability to reduce transmission costs by reducing demand during coincident
peak periods, large loads will have less incentive to invest in flexibility or voluntarily reduce demand when
the grid needs it most. In effect, the proposal risks converting flexible load into inflexible load. This
outcome is inconsistent with ERCOT’s growing need for flexible demand. As TAEBA stated in previous
comments, with more than 50 GW of large loads seeking to come onto the grid by 2030, the Commission
should encourage these entities to be flexible, maximizing ERCOT’s options to manage the grid. ERCOT has
already developed mechanisms to help encourage flexibility from large loads. Under the Batch Zero
framework, a Provisional Controllable Load Resource may be evaluated at defined low and maximum
consumption levels, while a Withdrawal-Limited Private Use Network may combine a large load with
onsite generation subject to an enforceable withdrawal limit at the point of interconnection. ERCOT has
explained that these arrangements can accommodate load growth while reducing incremental transmission
dependency by netting onsite generation against load.3 The minimum billing demand would greatly reduce
the value of these arrangements by charging a customer with dependable onsite capacity as though the
transmission system must serve its entire load under all conditions. TAEBA would remind the commission that




1. CoBank, The State of Large Load Rate Design: Insights from the Delta Database,
https://www.cobank.com/knowledge-exchange/the-state-of-large-load-rate-design-insights-from-the-delta-
database.
2. Ibid.
3. ERCOT Comments on NPRR 1325 and PGRR 145, June 2025 Board Meeting, Item 15.1.4.3,
https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2026/05/24/15.1.4.3-ERCOT-Comments-on-NPRR1325-and-PGRR145.pdf




                                                                          Texas Advanced Energy Business Alliance   2
 demand flexibility helps maintain reliability during times of system stress, reduces electric prices by taking
demand off the grid during peaks, and can defer the need for further transmission upgrades.

TAEBA recognizes that all customers should pay their fair share of transmission costs. However, large loads
are already subject to significant obligations through other sections of this proposal and in Project No.
58481, Rulemaking to Implement Large Load Interconnection Standards. These include financial security
requirements, nonrefundable interconnection costs, and Contributions in Aid of Construction. These
mechanisms already help ensure large loads pay their fair share without removing the incentive for
demand response.

TAEBA is aware that some parties have raised concerns that large load participation in CP-based
transmission rates could shift costs to customers that cannot currently respond to price signals, such as
residential customers. However, this concern is not inherent to the CP methodology itself, but rather reflects
limitations in current rate design. As Chairman Darby stated in his letter to the Commission, “[t]he logical
next step is to authorize residential customers, through their REPs, to participate in demand-based
transmission rates. Doing so would close the remaining gap in equitable cost allocation, honor the
Legislature’s directive, and ensure that the families of Texas share the same rate-management tools that
have long been available to large commercial customers.”4 TAEBA agrees with Chairman Darby’s
assessment and encourages the Commission to pursue this option. Expanding access to CP participation
would allow more customers to benefit from demand response opportunities, reduce system peak demand,
and mitigate perceived cost shifts.

TAEBA also supports preserving the proposed exclusion of wholesale storage load from DSP 12CP load
and ERCOT 12CP load. Wholesale storage resources should not be discouraged through transmission cost
allocation rules that could undermine their ability to provide reliability, flexibility, and market benefits to
ERCOT. To the extent the Commission includes block load transfers in DSP 12CP and ERCOT 12CP load,
the Commission should ensure that such treatment avoids double recovery and accurately assigns
responsibility to the load being served.

Answers to Staff Questions

1. Should the values associated with the large load minimum billing demand provisions be different
for large load customers with different contracted peak demands or different noncoincident (NCP)
demands?




4. Chairman Darby letter to the Public Utility Commission of Texas, Project No. 58000, Item No. 5,
https://interchange.puc.texas.gov/search/documents/?controlNumber=58000&itemNumber=5.


                                                                            Texas Advanced Energy Business Alliance   3
 TAEBA opposes the large load minimum billing demand as currently proposed. However, if the Commission
adopts a minimum billing demand, it should avoid a rigid, one-size-fits-all approach. Different minimum
billing demand values may be appropriate for large load customers with materially different capacity
reservations, risk profiles, energization schedules, or demonstrated flexibility capabilities.

TAEBA does not support using NCP demand as the primary basis for setting minimum billing demand
values. NCP demand is not necessarily tied to ERCOT system peaks or transmission cost causation. If
differentiated values are adopted, they should be based on objective cost-causation principles, the
customer’s actual reservation of transmission capacity, and the customer’s ability to reduce load during
periods of system stress.

2. Should the large load minimum billing demand be fixed for 20 years as proposed, reduced in
phases over a period of 20 years, or extended to a longer time period?

Of these options, TAEBA recommends that any large load minimum billing demand be reduced in phases,
rather than fixed for 20 years or extended for a longer period. A phased reduction would better
preserve incentives for flexibility.

However, the minimum billing demand should not start at 100% of contracted demand, and the
Commission should consider reducing the period of time to less than 20 years. A 20-year obligation could
cover nearly the entire lifecycle of a data center project and may be overly burdensome, potentially
discouraging investment in Texas and shifting too much development risk onto large load customers.

3. Should the large load minimum billing demand be based on some measure of demand lower than
contracted peak demand and NCP demand?

Yes. If the Commission adopts a large load minimum billing demand, it should be based on a measure
lower than 100% of contracted peak demand or NCP demand. There would be little incentive for large
loads to participate in demand reduction if minimum billing demand remains at 100% of contracted load.

The Commission’s proposed minimum billing demand is also out of step with other large load tariff
proposals. According to a database of emerging large load tariffs, only 33 of 77 filings included minimum
billing requirements.5 Of those 33 filings, the average minimum billing demand was 80%, significantly
below the 100% level proposed here.6 Maintaining a 100% minimum billing demand would discourage



5. CoBank, The State of Large Load Rate Design: Insights from the Delta Database,
https://www.cobank.com/knowledge-exchange/the-state-of-large-load-rate-design-insights-from-the-delta-
database.
6. Ibid.


                                                                         Texas Advanced Energy Business Alliance   4
 flexible load participation and could push large load investment to states with less burdensome tariff
structures.

TAEBA does not support relying on NCP demand as the primary basis for minimum billing demand because
NCP demand is not necessarily tied to ERCOT system peaks or transmission cost causation. If a minimum
billing demand is adopted, a ratcheted approach based on a percentage of contracted peak demand
would be simpler and more transparent than a weighted-average approach. That percentage should start
below 100% and decline over time to preserve incentives for large loads to invest in flexibility and reduce
demand during peak system conditions.

4. Should separate rate treatment be applied to a large computational load?

No. TAEBA does not recommend separate rate treatment based solely on whether a large load is
classified as “large computational load.” Rate treatment should be based on cost causation, actual system
impact, reserved capacity, interconnection requirements, and the customer’s ability to provide flexibility -
not the customer’s business model or end-use technology.

The Commission has authority to establish customer classifications and rates, but those rates must remain just
and reasonable and may not be unreasonably preferential, prejudicial, or discriminatory. Accordingly,
any separate treatment for large computational loads should be supported by a clear evidentiary record
showing that such loads impose materially different costs or operational impacts on the transmission system
than other similarly situated large loads.

Large computational loads may differ significantly in how they operate. For example, a large load with
onsite resources, storage, or contractual curtailment capability may have a very different impact on the
grid than a similarly sized load without those capabilities. If the Commission determines that some
differentiated treatment is necessary, it should be technology-neutral and tied to objective factors such as
contracted peak demand, demonstrated flexibility, energization schedule, contribution to system peaks,
and transmission upgrades directly caused by the customer.

5. Should the definition for transmission interconnection costs be broadened to include transmission
projects that are recommended at the conclusion of a batch study to serve the transmission capacity
needs of a particular load?

TAEBA does not recommend broadly expanding the definition of transmission interconnection costs to
automatically include all transmission projects recommended at the conclusion of a batch study.
Transmission projects identified through a batch study may provide broader reliability, load-serving, or
system benefits beyond a single large load customer. Automatically treating those projects as



                                                                       Texas Advanced Energy Business Alliance   5
 interconnection costs could improperly assign network-upgrade costs to individual customers even where the
facilities ultimately benefit the broader transmission system.

However, if a project is clearly and directly attributable to a particular large load, and the record
demonstrates that the project is needed primarily to serve that customer’s specific capacity reservation
rather than broader system needs, the Commission could consider targeted cost assignment. Any such
treatment should be based on transparent, objective cost-causation criteria and should avoid double
recovery from both the large load customer and transmission ratepayers.

6. If a large load customer is able to reserve transmission capacity irrespective of whether the large
load customer has energized or is fully using available capacity, how should these loads be reflected
in resource adequacy reports and assessments and transmission planning studies?

Reserved transmission capacity should be reflected in resource adequacy reports, assessments, and
transmission planning studies, but it should be clearly distinguished from actual energized load and actual
metered demand. If a large load customer has reserved capacity but has not energized or is not fully
using that capacity, treating the full reserved amount as actual demand could overstate near-term demand
and distort resource adequacy assessments.

At the same time, reserved capacity should not be ignored. If a large load has made binding financial
commitments and transmission capacity is being planned or held for that customer, ERCOT and transmission
planners should account for that reservation in forward-looking studies. However, reports and studies
should separately identify actual metered load, energized but not fully ramped load, reserved capacity
with binding commitments, and speculative or uncommitted future load.

To the extent a large load customer has enforceable flexibility, curtailment capability, or demand
response commitments, those capabilities should also be reflected in planning assumptions. Flexible large
loads should not be modeled the same way as fully firm, inflexible load if they can reliably reduce
demand during system stress.

Conclusion

TAEBA thanks the Commission for the opportunity to provide comments on this proposal. TAEBA looks
forward to continued engagement with the Commission, Commission Staff, ERCOT, and stakeholders to
ensure that transmission cost recovery policies protect customers, preserve efficient price signals, and
encourage flexible load participation that supports ERCOT reliability.




                                                                        Texas Advanced Energy Business Alliance   6
                    Respectfully submitted,


          /s/ Jonathan Amthor, Associate
Texas Advanced Energy Business Alliance

              (781) 908.3477 Ext: 3212
     P.O. Box 301151, Austin, TX 78703

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF TAEBA’S COMMENTS IN RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF’S PROPOSAL

TAEBA provides the Commission with the following recommendations:

   •   Maintain a coincident peak methodology for transmission cost allocation.
   •   Recognize that 12CP remains acceptable, while 5CP would better preserve targeted peak-
       reduction incentives.
   •   Reject the proposed 100% contracted peak demand minimum billing demand.
   •   If a minimum billing demand is adopted, set it below 100% of contracted peak demand and
       phase it down over time.
   •   Avoid extending the minimum billing demand beyond 20 years and consider a shorter duration.
   •   Do not rely on NCP demand as the primary basis for minimum billing demand.
   •   Preserve incentives for large loads to reduce demand during coincident peak periods.
   •   Do not apply separate rate treatment to large computational load based solely on business model
       or end-use technology.
   •   Ensure any differentiated rate treatment is technology-neutral, cost-based, and supported by a
       clear evidentiary record.
   •   Do not broadly expand transmission interconnection costs to automatically include all batch-study
       transmission projects.
   •   Preserve the proposed exclusion of wholesale storage load from DSP 12CP load and ERCOT
       12CP load.
   •   Ensure any treatment of block load transfers avoids double recovery and accurately assigns
       responsibility to the load being served.
   •   Reflect reserved transmission capacity in planning and resource adequacy studies, but distinguish it
       from actual energized load and actual metered demand.
   •   Reflect enforceable flexibility, curtailment capability, and demand response commitments in
       planning assumptions.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF TAEBA'S COMMENTS IN RESPONSE TO COMMISSION STAFF'S PROPOSAL

TAEBA provides the Commission with the following recommendations:

        •   Maintain a coincident peak methodology for transmission cost allocation.
        •   Recognize that 12CP remains acceptable, while 5CP would better preserve targeted peak-
            reduction incentives.
        •   Reiect the proposed 100% contracted peak demand minimum billing demand.

        •   If a minimum billing demand is adopted, set it below 100% of contracted peak demand and
            phase it down over time.
        •   Avoid extending the minimum billing demand beyond 20 years and consider a shorter duration.
        •   Do not rely on NCP demand as the primary basis for minimum billing demand.
        •   Preserve incentives for large loads to reduce demand during coincident peak periods.

        •   Do not apply separate rate treatment to large computational load based solely on business model
            or end-use technology.
        •   Ensure any differentiated rate treatment is technology-neutral, cost-based, and supported by a
            clear evidentiary record.
        •   Do not broadly expand transmission interconnection costs to automatically include all batch-study
            transmission proiects.
        •   Preserve the proposed exclusion of wholesale storage load from DSP 12CP load and ERCOT
            12CP load.
        •   Ensure any treatment of block load transfers avoids double recovery and accurately assigns
            responsibility to the load being served.
        •   Reflect reserved transmission capacity in planning and resource adequacy studies, but distinguish it
            from actual energized load and actual metered demand.
        •   Reflect enforceable flexibility, curtailment capability, and demand response commitments in
            planning assumptions.
